editorial:
Imagine starting a home movie with your buddies and not finishing it for nearly twenty years. That is exactly what happens here. You get to follow Dexter Romweber and his drummer, Crow, as they hit the road on a rock and roll tour. At first, it feels like a fun, old-school trip captured in black and white. It has a raw, gritty energy that makes you feel like you are riding in the van with them. You see the hope and excitement of two guys just trying to make it big in the music world, which gives the start of the film a really light and hopeful spirit.

Once the film jumps forward seventeen years, things get way more serious. You see the real cost of fame, including bad drug habits and deep sadness. The contrast between the young, happy musicians and the older, tired versions of themselves is what makes this so powerful. While the pacing can feel a bit slow because it covers so much time, the honesty is refreshing.
endingExplained: The movie ends by showing where Dexter and Crow stand after all those years of struggle. It wraps up by blending the old footage with the new, showing that while they didn't become global superstars, their music survived. You see them reflecting on their mistakes and their losses. It finishes on a bittersweet note, proving that art is often more important than money or fame in the long run.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves music history and honest stories about struggle.
